Write at least 2000 words explaining how language models generate text, how memory bandwidth affects speed, and how speculative decoding verifies proposals. Continue in detailed paragraphs with examples.

result.text:
The generation of text by large language models (LLMs) is a complex computational process that bridges the gap between abstract mathematical representations and human-readable language. At its core, an LLM is a neural network trained on vast amounts of textual data to predict the next token in a sequence. This process, often referred to as autoregressive generation, involves transforming input text into numerical embeddings, passing these embeddings through multiple layers of attention mechanisms and feed-forward networks, and finally projecting the resulting hidden states back into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Understanding this mechanism requires dissecting the architecture, the computational bottlenecks, and the optimization techniques that allow these models to operate efficiently in real-world applications.

To begin with, the fundamental operation of an LLM relies on the transformer architecture, which was introduced in 2017 and has since become the standard for natural language processing. When a user inputs a prompt, the model first tokenizes the text, breaking it into discrete units such as words, subwords, or characters. These tokens are then mapped to high-dimensional vectors known as embeddings. These embeddings capture semantic meaning, allowing the model to understand relationships between words, such as the similarity between "king" and "queen" or the syntactic structure of a sentence. Once embedded, the data flows through a series of transformer blocks. Each block consists primarily of two components: a self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward network. The self-attention mechanism allows the model to weigh the importance of different tokens in the context relative to each other. For example, in the sentence "The cat sat on the mat," the attention mechanism helps the model understand that "sat" is related to "cat" and "mat," establishing a coherent semantic link. This process is repeated across dozens or even hundreds of layers, progressively refining the representation of the input until the final layer produces a hidden state vector. This vector is then projected onto the vocabulary space, generating a probability distribution for the next token. The model selects the token with the highest probability, or samples from the distribution, and appends it to the sequence. This process repeats iteratively, generating text one token at a time.

However, the speed at which this generation occurs is not solely determined by the complexity of the neural network calculations. A critical factor influencing performance is memory bandwidth. In modern computing, the central processing unit (CPU) or graphics processing unit (GPU) must fetch data from memory to perform computations. For LLMs, the primary bottleneck during inference is often not the arithmetic operations themselves
